opening.headline: Among problems that cannot be followed no matter how many times the same instructions are repeated, tuning determines which ones can be solved and which ones cannot.
body: Even though I keep adding rules to the prompt, the JSON key name sometimes changes, or I add tone guidelines, but only some responses come out stiffly. These repetitive errors often do not go away with more instructions.

In this lesson, we'll look at what tuning changes in a model and contrast good and bad cases. In particular, it explains why attempts at tuning to incorporate new knowledge fail, and summarizes the prerequisites that must be met before deciding on tuning.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain what problems tuning solves and what problems it does not solve
Can distinguish cases where tuning is appropriate

screens.title: Even if instructions are written dozens of times, they are not followed.
screens.lead: A team's prompts are getting longer and longer, but the same error remains. Read on for three repetition errors.

visual.alt: A scene showing a prompt document that is getting longer and three pieces of output that are still misaligned side by side.
labels: JSON with occasionally changed key names
Some parts of the writing style are stiff.

paragraphs: One team operates a function that receives responses as JSON. I keep adding rules to the prompt, but the key names change sometimes. Also, even though guidelines for a polite tone were included, only some responses were written in a stiff style. Responses that skip the established judgment process are also sometimes mixed.

All three errors are not due to lack of information. The information you need is already in the input, what's lacking is consistent action. OpenAI's Accuracy Optimization Guide categorizes cases where the format, tone is incorrect, or the reasoning is not followed consistently are problems with LLM optimization, or behavioral axis.

These repetitive errors are often not easily captured by prompts. Increasing the number of instructions results in longer prompts, which increases costs and does not increase consistency significantly. This class identifies how tuning solves these problems and which problems it cannot solve.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What do all three errors have in common: new information or consistent action? We will answer this question at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let's think of items that are never followed in your work.

screens.title: Think of items that are never followed
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think of it first and then press it.

items.prompt: Are there any items that are not followed even if you repeat the same instructions dozens of times?
items.answer: If so, it is likely that the item is of a type that is difficult for the model to consistently follow, not because of a lack of expressive instructions. First, check whether you have written enough instructions and examples for that item, and if it is still repeated, it becomes a candidate for tuning.

items.prompt: Is the item closer to form, tone, or judgment criteria?
items.answer: All three are representative areas that tuning addresses. Format is a matter of fixing the output structure, tone is a matter of speech and style, and judgment criteria is a matter of consistency in reaching the same conclusion from the same input.

items.prompt: Was the information needed for that item already in the input?
items.answer: This question is the most important. If the information wasn't in the input, it's not a matter of tuning, it's a matter of injecting context. If the information is there but the method is shaky, it's a behavioral issue and tuning may be a candidate.

screens.outro: Now let's take a step-by-step look at what tuning changes in the model.

screens.title: What Tuning Does: Learn Behavior
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to move through the steps and see how the actions instructed by the prompt are translated into learning.

visual.alt: Flowchart of training a pre-trained model on example data to obtain a model that maintains its format even with short prompts.
labels: Example of input and output of correct answer

steps.title: Step 1: State instructed by prompt
steps.body: Initially, match the model's behavior by adding long instructions and a few-shot examples to each prompt. The same instructions are repeated as input tokens for each request, but sometimes the format is not correct. The model itself does not remember these instructions, so you have to remind them each time.

steps.title: Step 2: Prepare example data
steps.body: Tuning is the task of additionally training the already trained model with examples of input and correct output for our purpose. So, first, we prepare example data in the same format as the actual input. The OpenAI guide explains that this dataset preparation is the most important step.

steps.title: Step 3: Practice learning
steps.body: Run the training task on the examples you prepared. After training, the new tuning model can be used for inference. To check performance after learning, you must set aside evaluation data that was not used for learning to detect overfitting.

steps.title: Step 4: Solidify your actions
steps.body: The OpenAI documentation explains that tuning can help ensure that responses are in a consistent format and that new inputs are treated in the same way. This is learned memory. Because the example is repeated and solidified into action, the format can be maintained without having to include lengthy instructions in the prompt.

steps.title: Step 5: Benefits and Presuppositions of Efficiency
steps.body: The OpenAI guide explains two reasons for tuning: The goal is to increase the accuracy of a specific task, and achieve the same accuracy with fewer tokens or a smaller model. However, tuning is a time-consuming task, so a baseline of evaluation and prompts must be in place first.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen what tuning changes, let's take a look at which problems are suitable and which are not.

screens.title: Tuning good and bad cases
screens.lead: The table below juxtaposes cases where tuning works and cases where it does not. As you read each line, pay attention to the reason in the last column.

data.caption: Problems that are suitable for tuning and problems that are not suitable for tuning
rows: Format fixation
JSON key names and field order change from response to response
fit
The information is already there, only the method of output is shaken. If you repeatedly learn examples of the correct answer format, the structure becomes fixed.
tone and style
Even with polite tone guidelines, some responses are stiff.
fit
It is difficult to describe speaking style with rules, and it is more effective to show it with examples. Learn examples of responses with the same tone.
Consistency of judgment criteria
Classify inquiries of the same type into different categories
fit
Classification is a representative use cited in OpenAI's map fine-tuning document. Match the criteria with examples with correct answer labels.
Correction of failure to follow instructions
Even if you give enough instructions, you keep missing certain instructions.
fit
The purpose of the same document is to correct failure to follow instructions. Learn examples of correctly executed responses.
new latest knowledge
Make the model reflect the company regulations that changed last month
unsuitable
Tuning is a way to change behavior, not a way to update it. For these problems, search provides context.
data.notes: The OpenAI documentation explains that supervised fine-tuning is suitable for classification, nuanced translation, generating content in specific formats, and correcting failures to follow instructions. Google Cloud Documents also includes classification, summarization, abstract Q&A, and dialogue as effective tasks. Common conditions are the presence of well-defined tasks and labeled data. Conversely, if the cause is a lack of information, tuning is not a prescription. When reading the table, look at the causes, not the names of the cases. If the information is in the input but the method is shaky, it is suitable. If the information itself is not in the input, it is unsuitable. Tasks with clear answers, such as classification or format fixation, are easier to evaluate, making it easier to check the difference before and after tuning. Conversely, for tasks where there is no single correct answer, such as tone, the criteria for a good response should be written down first. The fifth row of the table is the most important border for this lesson. Even if you train the same model with the same data, it is effective if the goal is action, but it is not effective if the goal is knowledge.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the criteria for determining suitability, let's explain the most common failure cases.

screens.title: Explanation: Why does tuning to add new knowledge fail?
screens.lead: The instructor explains a team's attempt step by step. Select the arrow to the right to view the results in the following order: Attempts, Results, Causes, and Correct Prescription. Learners do not enter answers.

steps.title: Try: Convert regulatory documents into training data
steps.body: One team converted hundreds of in-house regulatory documents into tuning data in the form of questions and answers for training. The expectation was that the model would memorize the company regulations and answer the questions. This effort also involves reading the document and converting it into questions and answers.

steps.title: Result: Sounds good at first, but soon goes wrong
steps.body: Some questions had compliant answers. However, when the regulations were revised, the model still answered with the content at the time of learning, and plausible answers were made up for regulations that were not in the training data.

steps.title: Cause 1: Model is stuck on training point values
steps.body: The information changes, but the model remains fixed at the value at the time it was learned. Every time regulations change, data must be recreated and retrained. The correct way to transfer knowledge that changes is through input.

steps.title: Cause 2: Learning to make up information that doesn’t exist
steps.body: OpenAI's tuning best practices state that training examples should contain the information needed to respond. For example, by learning examples that praise user characteristics that are not in the input, the model can learn to invent information. The example of trying to get people to memorize the rules runs this very risk.

steps.title: Classification criteria: lack of information or consistent action?
steps.body: The OpenAI guide distinguishes between using search augmentation when information is insufficient and tuning when consistent behavior is needed. The problem for this team was that they didn't know that the model was prescriptive, so it was a context axis problem from the beginning.

steps.title: Correct prescription: knowledge through search, action through tuning
steps.body: Regulations are found through search and entered into the input, and actions to consistently provide answers in the form of regulation citations are adjusted if necessary. The two methods are additive, so they can be used together in one use case. The key is to let each person focus on his or her own problems. By dividing roles in this way, even if the regulations are revised, only the documents in the repository need to be changed, and there is no need to retrain the model.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the cause of the failure, we will summarize the conditions that must be met before starting tuning.

screens.title: Preconditions for tuning judgment
screens.lead: As you select and expand each item, you will see why the condition is needed. Open all four items.

items.title: There is an evaluation set so you can compare before and after.
items.body: OpenAI documentation advises to evaluate first and then invest in tuning. This is because there must be a reliable way to determine whether the tuned model is better than the base model. The evaluation should consist of inputs that are likely to be seen in actual operations.

items.title: Establish a baseline with prompts and examples
items.body: The results of the prompt step serve as the baseline. Without a baseline, you can't tell the effectiveness of your tuning, and you may spend unnecessary money on problems that could have been solved with a prompt.

items.title: Training examples are in the same format as actual input.
items.body: OpenAI best practices state that all training examples should be in the format expected for inference. If the format is different between training and actual use, the behavior learned by the model will not appear properly.

items.title: Quality of examples is more important than quantity
items.body: The same article says that if you have to choose between the two, small amounts of high-quality data are more effective than large amounts of low-quality data. If the data is created by multiple people, the degree of agreement between people may be the upper limit of model performance.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the conditions, we will summarize today's standards on the final screen.

screens.title: Tuning changes behavior, it doesn't change knowledge
screens.lead: We organize the lesson by answering the question posed at the beginning: whether new information or consistent action is needed for the three repetitive errors.

paragraphs: The first three errors I saw were variations in JSON key names, the stiff tone of some responses, and inferences that skipped steps. All the information needed was in the input and what was lacking was consistent behavior. So tuning becomes a candidate.

Tuning is a method of solidifying the format, tone, and judgment criteria by learning examples of input and correct output. It is effective when the task is well-defined and has labeled data, such as classification, generating a specific format, or correcting failure to follow instructions. In terms of efficiency, tokens can be reduced by replacing long instructions with learning.

Conversely, attempting to inject up-to-date information or private knowledge into the model is an inappropriate use of tuning. The model is fixed at the values ​​at the time of training, and can learn to invent examples if the required information is not available. It is correct to solve these problems through search.

Before making any tuning decisions, you need an evaluation set and a prompt baseline. Training examples should be in the same format as the actual input, and quality is more important than quantity. Only when this condition is met can the before and after tuning be compared using the same criteria.

There is one last sentence to remember. If a problem requires the model to learn something new, it is solved through context, and if a problem requires the model to behave differently, it is solved through tuning. The habit of asking this question first will prevent you from choosing the wrong expensive path. Once a decision has been made, it is reviewed again if the evaluation results change.

callout.label: Based on one sentence
callout.text: Tuning changes behavior, it doesn't change knowledge. New knowledge is solved through search, and consistent actions are solved through tuning.

checks.intro: Think back and check the good and bad cases you just saw. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Which of the following problems is best suited for tuning?
options: Make the model reflect the company regulations that changed last month
Fix an issue where JSON key names change slightly from response to response
Answer the daily updated inventory quantity
Have them provide a list of newly hired employees.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. There is information, but the output format is unstable, so tuning is appropriate.
checks.incorrectFeedback: That's not the kind of problem that tuning can solve. Try to determine whether you need new information or consistent action.
checks.explain: Tuning is appropriate for behavioral issues such as format fixation, tone, and judgment consistency. Infusing up-to-date knowledge is an inappropriate use.

wrong.0: This is not appropriate because it involves fixing changing information to the value at the time of learning.
wrong.2: It is correct to provide information that changes frequently through search.
wrong.3: Since it is injection of private information, it is a search issue.

checks.intro: Please remember and check the reasons for the failure that you saw in the commentary. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: What is the most appropriate reason why attempts to learn by creating hundreds of in-house regulatory documents as tuning data are problematic?
options: Because tuning does not support JSONL format
This is because the output format is inevitably broken after learning.
Even if information changes, the model is fixed to the value at the time of learning.
Hundreds of tuning examples are too many.
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. Since changing knowledge is tied to the learning point value, it must be supplied through search.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The reason is not true. Recall the limitations of how tuning deals with knowledge.
checks.explain: The information changes, but the model is fixed at the value at the time of learning. Also, if you don't have the information you need for an example, you can learn how to make up information that doesn't exist.

wrong.0: JSONL is rather a tuning data format.
wrong.1: Tuning is a method used to make formatting consistent.
wrong.3: The large number of examples is not a reason.

checks.intro: Think of the prerequisites and put the steps in order to determine tuning. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Lay out the steps in order when deciding on tuning.
items: Establish an evaluation set to compare before and after
Establish a baseline with prompts and examples
Tuning with an example of the same format as the actual input
Compare before and after using the same evaluation set
checks.correctFeedback: We set the correct order that evaluation and baseline come before tuning.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Remember that you can't judge the effectiveness of a tuning without a baseline to compare it to.
checks.explain: You need an evaluation set and baseline to determine whether tuning actually helped.

glossary.def: This is a process of changing behavior by additionally learning inputs for each purpose and output examples of correct answers to an already learned model.
Repeat examples to ensure consistency in format, tone, and judgment. This corresponds to learned memory.
It trains the output structure so that it is the same every time.
This is data with a standard output corresponding to the input. Required for guided tuning.

misconceptions.myth: When we tune it, the model memorizes our documentation.
misconceptions.fact: Tuning is a way to change behavioral patterns. It is correct to enter the latest knowledge or private knowledge as input through search, and when learning a document, it is fixed to the value at the time of learning.

misconceptions.myth: Tuning is always more accurate than prompting.
misconceptions.fact: Without evaluation, you won’t know whether you are improving. First, you need to baseline with a prompt and compare before and after with the same set of assessments.
Small amounts of high-quality data are usually more effective than large amounts of low-quality data. If an example is missing necessary information, you can learn to make it up instead.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Tuning changes behavior, it doesn't change knowledge.
Consistency of format fixation, tone, and judgment criteria are appropriate areas for tuning.
Injecting new knowledge is an inappropriate use of tuning and is solved by search.
Before tuning, you need an evaluation set and a prompt baseline.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Does solving our problem require the model to learn something new or act differently?
